name: Yusuf Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play hand percussion for a small community theatre, record short drum cues and teach two beginners at the rehearsal room. I finished secondary school and came to paid music after years of warehouse shifts; at 58 I still ask our lead drummer to check a difficult entrance. I like hearing actors find their feet when a cue lands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps that work going at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works changing hours at a grocery shop and our children are grown, with their own bills. We rent a flat, and our savings cover about two weeks. There are few similar gigs nearby, so I cannot treat retirement as a date when work automatically stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stage manager that faster booking messages are welcome if a paid drummer is still on the show sheet. Someone has to hear the actor miss the beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks saved and my partner’s shifting grocery hours make a late show fee serious. A mild AI outcome does not solve the rent we owe next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid Saturday theatre sets, two pupils and small cue recordings this season. I use AI every day to sort calls, but I listen to the original sound before sending a cue; if a show cancels, I would skip the paid practice room that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary missed fees. Our grown children can visit, but I do not ask them to pay the flat rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a show cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall lost power in spring and our Saturday pay went with it. I would ask for a written half-fee cancellation term before the next season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check in an AI booking list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stage manager’s call sheet has the actual start time. A wrong hour can mean I miss a paid entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that generated drum cues could replace a small paid recording before a robot ever walks onstage. I would ask for written fees on live sets and revisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues are almost a third of my own music pay, and clients could stop ordering them. I can still play live. Two weeks saved cannot cover a long gap in paid theatre cues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for three months of written paid theatre calls and a paid engineer demonstration of a new AI drum-cleanup tool, which removes background noise from a recorded hit. In the first year I would test it on my own nameless take using the theatre’s licence and approved local storage, compare the cleaned hit with the original by ear, and stop if the beat changes or the file leaves the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if a third of my pay went without another paid route. I expect some cue orders to fall, and our rent leaves almost no time to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a pupil’s drum recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would use only a take I own. A young pupil’s sound and name stay out of a trial unless a family gives permission and storage is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay a subscription to keep using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the theatre must cover the trial licence and training hour. I would return to the original file if it charges me or changes the rhythm.

I would warn that **generated cues** threaten small recording jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that thinking AGI by 2028 could make a drum cue in seconds. Hands-on playing robots arrive around 2031, three years later, but my cue invoice could go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect cue orders to end in 2028 and some theatres may choose generated backing. A late recording fee is rent money to us; I cannot assume a retirement cheque arrives at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would count cue invoices and request a signed theatre calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid show nights fall too, I would seek a posted arts-centre sound assistant job only if my secondary schooling and stage experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel beats lost fees and the hours fit the bus route; I would keep paid sets and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about losing cues with almost no reserve and possible show cuts. I know where to apply, but that does not pay next month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 60 instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have not saved enough to stop earning in 2028, and I will not pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a manager only mentions an opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep playing and teaching. I need a posted vacancy, written hours and pay, and a signed offer before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stage manager that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn a paid sound role. Playing robots follow around 2034, after cue-making changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues might stop selling by 2031, when I will be 63. A live-sound qualification could help, but a free course is not a wage when rent is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the theatre workshop for a paid six-month sound-assistant place only if a real opening is offered, tuition is funded and the shifts do not replace my existing paid Saturday sets without equal wages. In the first year after 2031, if cue fees end, I would apply for a posted sound-assistant job only if the certificate qualifies me and its written net pay after travel replaces lost fees on a bus route I can work; I would keep pupils and booked sets until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until an actual paid place and job exist. Five years to prepare helps, but our two-week account cannot fund unpaid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wire a speaker alone on day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the theatre sound lead must supervise my first checks. I would not touch live wiring without their sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the place is funded but unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid Saturday sets and ask about the next paid intake. Free sound-course tuition will not cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to keep earning and learn a safer trade. Robots able to play drums follow around 2039, but no card tells me when rent stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need theatre and pupil fees. I cannot set a retirement day from a two-week reserve, even if we have a decade to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would save ten percent of each extra paid Saturday set after rent, food and bus fares toward one month of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep the paid sets and pupils that remain, then seek a posted arts-centre sound job only if show pay falls, I meet its actual requirements and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees on a reachable bus route; I would leave current work only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain anxious about near bills and later cue losses. A decade lets me prepare, but it does not turn two weeks of savings into retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra paid sets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing from that source. I cannot take a pretend fee out of the food envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept an unpaid title at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need posted paid hours and a written net wage that covers the lost theatre work after travel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue orders could end before I find another paying route. Signed theatre dates, a real paid sound place and a posted job with written net wages above lost fees would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a sound course pays while I am learning at 63. My rent will not wait for a certificate to dry.

headlineQuote: My rent will not wait for a certificate to dry.
portrait: At **58**, Yusuf is a junior hand percussionist with secondary schooling, grown children, a partner and only two weeks saved.
His **lower pay** comes from theatre sets, simple cues and two beginner pupils in an area with few similar jobs.
He uses **AI daily** for calls and tests new cleanup on owned sound after paid instruction and manual checks.
He seeks a **funded paid sound place** only if earnings continue, then posted qualified work with viable net pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end cue orders before a paid replacement job is real.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre dates**, a paid funded sound place and a posted eligible job with written net replacement pay would help.
